content.comment_body: Hello everyone, I am using a [company_name] [product_name] together with a [company_name] HMI panel for a basic application—just starting and stopping a few drives and managing some IO. Everything works, but I've reached a challenge with the alarms. From my research, it looks like this HMI panel only allows alarms to be triggered by words. Is there a way to convert a [product_name] bit to a word so the HMI panel can use it for triggering alarm messages? Or is this simply not achievable with this hardware combination?

Is your [product_name] also on [version_no]? You only mentioned the software version. Yes, it's possible—use the VM memory. For example: 1. Alarm = V101.0, 2. Alarm = V101.1, ..., 8. Alarm = V101.7, 9. Alarm = V100.0, ..., 16. Alarm = V100.7. In the alarm table, then use VW100.

Great, so this can be done—thank you for your update. My hardware is indeed [product_name] [version_no]. In the VM configuration, I can't see my fault relay coil (example: M32) to assign it to VW100. Is there a specific block I should use instead of a standard relay coil so it will show up in the VM configuration drop-down, or can it be done another way?
You don't need to assign the VM parameter separately. The V-bits from V100.0 to V101.7 are already part of the VW100 word. You can link M32 to the relevant V-bit through the digital network output.
Thanks for your help—that resolved the issue.

analysis.insight_summary: Forum users explored methods to link alarms from a [product_name] controller to an HMI panel. The main challenge was ensuring the HMI could trigger alarms via word signals, as bit-level outputs from the controller do not match the HMI's requirements. A user clarified that individual bits can be mapped to V-memory words, so alarms can be reliably configured. Discussion covered VM memory mapping and digital network output configuration.
analysis.user_expectations: Users are seeking a simple, effective way to assign [product_name] bit outputs to a word address for HMI alarm activation, without complex setups or requiring more advanced hardware.
